title: Participate in the development and management of an agri business plan

lessons.title: The parts of an agri-business plan
lessons.html:
Why a business plan?

A business plan sets out where the farm business is going, how it will get there and how much it will cost and earn. It is used to guide management, to apply for finance (banks, the Land Bank, development agencies) and to communicate with partners and staff. Supervisors and team leaders contribute information and help put the plan into action.

Typical contents

  1. Executive summary: a one-page overview, written last.
  2. Business description: location, land, enterprises, ownership and legal form (sole proprietor, partnership, company, co-operative, trust).
  3. Vision, mission and goals: specific, measurable goals such as "Increase avocado yield to the target tonnes per hectare within three seasons."
  4. Situation analysis: resources (land, water rights, infrastructure, equipment, people) and a SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats).
  5. Market plan: products, customers, channels, prices, competitors and promotion.
  6. Production plan: enterprise sizes, production calendar, inputs, expected yields, technology.
  7. Human resources plan: organisational structure, staffing, skills and training.
  8. Financial plan: enterprise budgets, cash flow forecast, projected income statement and balance sheet, capital needs and funding.
  9. Risk management: main risks and how they will be reduced.
  10. Implementation and monitoring: action plan, responsibilities and indicators.

SWOT example for a small vegetable enterprise

StrengthsWeaknesses
Reliable borehole, skilled teamNo cold room, old tractor
OpportunitiesThreats
Local school feeding contract, growing townDrought, theft, rising electricity costs

Strategies use strengths to grab opportunities and fix weaknesses that expose the business to threats.

lessons.title: Financial planning and managing the plan
lessons.html:
Enterprise budgets

For each enterprise, estimate gross income (yield multiplied by price) and variable costs (seed, fertiliser, chemicals, feed, packaging, transport, casual labour). The difference is the gross margin. Use realistic yields from farm records, not best-case figures.

Cash flow forecast

A cash flow shows money coming in and going out month by month. Farming is seasonal: costs are high at planting while income arrives at harvest. The cash flow shows when the farm needs an overdraft or production loan and how big it must be.

MonthCash inCash outNet
SeptemberR20 000R150 000minus R130 000
FebruaryR380 000R60 000R320 000

Projected statements

  • Income statement: total gross margin minus fixed costs (permanent wages, depreciation, insurance, interest) gives net profit.
  • Balance sheet: assets (land, machinery, livestock, stock, cash) and liabilities (loans, creditors); the difference is owner's equity.

Sensitivity analysis

Test what happens if the price falls by 10 percent or yield drops due to drought. If a small change wipes out profit, the plan is risky and needs adjustment, insurance or reserves.

Managing the plan

  • Break the plan into an action plan with tasks, dates, responsible people and budgets.
  • Keep accurate records: inputs used, hours worked, yields, sales and costs.
  • Compare actual results with the budget monthly (variance analysis) and explain big differences.
  • Report progress to management and lenders as agreed.
  • Update the plan at least yearly or when conditions change, such as a new market, drought or price shock.

Your contribution

Supervisors provide realistic production data, cost information, labour needs and practical insights. You also implement the plan in the field and flag problems early.

Key points

  • A business plan covers market, production, people, finance and risk.
  • A SWOT analysis guides strategy.
  • Enterprise budgets and cash flow forecasts show profit and funding needs.
  • Sensitivity analysis tests the plan against price and yield risks.
  • Monitor actual results against the plan and update it regularly.
